title: Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit

epigraph.quote: The improvement in margins has been slower than we had anticipated.
epigraph.author: Parag Satpute, MD & Group CEO, Greaves Cotton, Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026

web_blocks.text: A leading indicator is an operating number that moves before the income statement does. Greaves is three businesses under one roof: engines, gensets and components sold to manufacturers and dealers (the core); an electric two-wheeler and three-wheeler maker (GEML, Greaves Electric Mobility Limited); and a small electric-vehicle lender (GFL, Greaves Finance Limited). Each has its own early-warning signal, so one blended ratio would mislead. We track six, because management discloses them every quarter and each changes before profit or cash does. [1][4]

web_blocks.caption: Six operating KPIs that lead the financials (latest disclosed values; VAHAN is the government vehicle-registration database)
rows: GEML e-2W billing volume and VAHAN share
37,649 units in Q2 FY27 (+114%); H1 FY27 62,944 (+116%); VAHAN share 4.8% against 4.1% in H1 FY26 [1][62]
Net revenue is about ₹93,100 a unit, so volume sets GEML revenue directly. Registrations show real end demand.
GEML EBITDA per unit and utilisation
−₹6,300 a unit against −₹20,000 a year earlier; plant about 40% used; 418 dealers selling 25 units a month each, up from 18 [1][62]
Fixed costs spread over more units, so the loss per unit shrinks. It shows when GEML can fund itself.
Medium-horsepower (MHP, 160–750 kVA) gensets ₹230 crore in H1 FY27 against ₹171 crore (+35%); aftermarket ₹77 crore (+15%) [1]
MHP is where Greaves is gaining ground; spares and service carry higher margins.
+48% in Q4 FY26, +36% in Q1 FY27, +37% in Q2 FY27; diesel three-wheeler OEM sales 42% of Mobility Solutions [26][25][1]
Engine shipments reach OEM lines within a quarter, and the end market is shrinking [70].
Core EBITDA margin and raw-material cost
Core EBITDA margin 11.5% in Q2 FY27 against 14.8%; raw materials 68.9% of revenue against 64.4% [1]
Metal prices hit costs at once, while OEM contracts reprice with a lag [24].
H1 FY27 inventories ₹314.32 crore to ₹455.19 crore; receivables ₹344.81 crore to ₹416.65 crore; operating cash flow −₹211.82 crore; debtor days 37 in FY26 against 42 [2][60]
Stock and receivables swell before sales turn into cash.
web_blocks.takeaway: Read together, the six say the same thing in two voices. Volumes and share are moving the right way in every business, so demand is not the problem [1]. Margin and cash are moving the wrong way, so conversion of that demand into profit is the open question, and the next two quarters of raw-material cost and receivable days will settle it [24]. Management expects commodity pass-through to reach the full company by Q4 FY27, which gives a date to test the margin claim against.

web_blocks.text: Two secondary signals matter. Excel Controlinkage, the Nagpur cable-and-lever maker, fell 6% in FY26, then grew 14% in Q1 FY27 and 30% in Q2 on new orders from Tata Motors' international business, CAT (UK) and TAFE [3][1][61]. Management also aimed to onboard 3,000 aftermarket retailers by FY27 from about 350, but the next deck gives no updated count [26][3]. We treat that target as unverified.

Capacity and runway. Greaves discloses installed capacity only for its electric businesses. For engines, gensets, cables and industrial engines, capacity and utilisation are not disclosed in anything we read [1][6]. Market sizes are patchy too: the genset figures come from a trade tracker and a research page, and the three-wheeler engine pool has no sourced size [79][91].

web_blocks.caption: Capacity and market runway by business (capacity in units a year unless stated; third-party market sizes are indicative)
rows: Industry 1,51,634 diesel gensets in FY25; Mahindra Powerol 23.8% [79]. Greaves about 4% [30][29]. Management cites 10–12% market growth for five years [27]; one research house puts 2026 at USD 2.1 billion, growing 6.9% a year [91].
Headroom from a 4% base. Limits: the top-horsepower engine is bought in, no data-centre franchise, and five players hold 55–60% of organised revenue [62][90].
Diesel three-wheeler engines are “continuously shrinking” [70]. L5 three-wheelers were about 8 lakh units in FY26 (+17%), electric about 33% [6].
Share of a shrinking pool, plus exports: Greaves is sole engine supplier to a French microcar maker [62].
Market size not disclosed; about 40% of FY22 revenue was exports [38].
Growth rests on new OEM wins; nothing to test it against.
FM/UL-listed fire-fighting engines; farm equipment exited over Chinese imports [24].
Small niche; −5% in H1 FY27, +9% like-for-like [1].
4,80,000 e-2W a year at Ranipet; 18,000 L5 a year at Toopran [1]
E-2W industry about 1.4 million units in FY26 (+21%) [6]; about 2.24 lakh registrations in October 2026 (+48%), Ampere 4.84% [85][84]. L5 subsidy closed 26 December 2025 [55].
Plenty of plant room, little share. Growth needs wins against TVS, Bajaj, Hero and Ather [84].
web_blocks.takeaway: The runway is lopsided. Genset and e-2W markets are large and growing, but Greaves holds about 4–5% of each, so volume is available if it can win it [79][84]. Diesel engines are the opposite: Greaves leads a pool that regulators and buyers are shrinking, so the highest-margin business has no volume tailwind [70]. That is why Excel, gensets and exports matter more than headline engine growth.

web_blocks.text: A utilisation cross-check. Management says GEML's utilisation is “about 40%” of roughly 40,000 units a month [62]. Q2 billing of 37,649 units over three months is about 12,550 a month, or about 31% of 40,000 (our arithmetic), so the 40% figure probably describes recent months; the filings do not say. Either way GEML can triple volume without a new factory, so its funding question is working capital and operating losses, not capacity.

The walk-the-talk record. Greaves held eleven earnings calls between May 2024 and October 2026. In August 2024 the then CFO said “as a corporate policy, we do not give future guidance” [33]. By November 2025 Greaves.Next set a 16–20% organic growth target, with a ₹15,000 crore vision behind it [28]. We scored only promises whose result can be read from a filing, using three words: MET, PARTLY and MISSED.

Core EBITDA margin held “where we are today”

Group EBITDA margin 5.8% to 6.2%, but core margin fell from about 12.7% to 11.5% (Q1 core EBITDA ₹178 crore less ₹88 crore, over revenue ₹1,478 crore less ₹768 crore) [1][3]
web_blocks.takeaway: Three promises were met, five partly met and two missed. Promises about the old engine business (margin, diesel demand, growth rate) have mostly been kept, except the standalone ROCE target of 50% plus, which was missed. Promises about the new businesses and the group's financial structure (GEML funding route, group margin) have slipped [6][4]. Open items still running are the H2 FY27 margin improvement, GEML breakeven “fairly soon”, no GEML funding for 12–18 months, and no further write-offs [24].

web_blocks.text: Words matter as much as outcomes. In October 2026 Satpute said the corrective actions “started showing results, but continued cost inflation has offset some of these gains” [24]. That is candid. Vikas Singh said of GEML: “Not in a position to give you an exact timeline, but we are running ahead of plan” [24]. A promise with no date cannot be scored. The CFO, Manish Poddar, said “there’s nothing more at this stage for any further write-offs,” then added that the review “will continue to happen” each quarter [62][24]. Both are true at once, so we do not read the first as a guarantee.

rows: Board vision cited on the Q3 and Q4 FY25 calls [31][30]
(15,000 ÷ 3,436.62) raised to 0.25, minus 1; an analyst on the call said “around 50%” [28]
Core FY30 at 16% and 20% a year
Greaves.Next organic target applied for four years [28]
Left for GEML, GFL and acquisitions
FY26 GEML revenue ₹786 crore [6] compounded four years
about ₹6,455 crore to ₹7,156 crore, or 26 to 28 Excel-sized businesses
Gap above less GEML at 40%; Excel FY26 revenue ₹252 crore [6]
web_blocks.takeaway: Management's own words give the route: “the CAGR of the core businesses added to the M&A strategically that we will do, plus the growth of the investee companies should take us towards our stated ambition” [28]. The organic plan covers well under half of the target, and even a GEML growing 40% a year leaves acquisitions to supply about twice today's group revenue. A ₹500–700 crore investment budget sits on the strategy slide, though that label was recovered from slide text and is indicative [4][1]. The largest cheque actually written, Excel, carried a maximum enterprise value of ₹385 crore [38].

web_blocks.text: Our credibility judgment. The case for management is strong in one area. The core engine business has held a 13–14% standalone EBITDA margin for three years, revenue is at a ten-year high, Q2 FY27 broadly matched the August call, and the CEO, CFO, CTO and GEML head were all refreshed within about a year, so these are new people measured against partly inherited promises [6][1]. The CFO also disclosed bad news in full: core net cash of ₹110 crore sits beside group borrowings of ₹513 crore and cash of ₹606 crore, and the filings say which is which [62][1].

The case against is also specific. The two promises with the largest financial consequence, standalone ROCE of 50% plus and an IPO-funded GEML, were not delivered. Group operating cash flow was −₹211.82 crore in H1 FY27 while margin recovery ran slower than planned [2][24]. Write-offs recur: ₹334.83 crore of net exceptional loss in FY24, ₹39.34 crore in FY26 and ₹60.1 crore of one-offs in Q2 FY27 [8][6][2]. Investors asked for a core-versus-GEML profit split and a revenue bridge, which suggests earlier reporting was harder to read than it needed to be [1].

Weighing both sides, we rate management credible on operations, unproven on capital allocation and timelines. Numbers management controls directly, such as plant output, launches and customer wins, have mostly landed. Numbers that depend on a commodity cycle, a subsidy regime or a regulator's calendar have often slipped, and direction without dates leaves little to hold the company to. Our probability read: 16–20% core growth is more likely than not to be roughly met over the next two years; a return to 14–15% core margin by FY28 is plausible but depends on the pass-through lag closing; GEML breakeven has no date; and ₹15,000 crore by FY30 is, on the arithmetic above, well under a one-in-ten outcome. What would change this view: core margin back above 14% in H2 FY27, a first quarter of positive GEML EBITDA, and operating cash flow that turns positive without help from payables.

book_paragraphs: Imagine you are on the investor call of a mid-sized Indian engine maker on a late-October afternoon in 2026. The chief executive has just told the line what you already suspected from the numbers. Revenue is up a fifth. Profit margin is not. And then he says something most executives never say aloud: the improvement in margins has been slower than we had anticipated. You and I have a choice at that moment. We can take the candour as a sign of an honest team, or we can ask what else was promised that has not yet arrived. The honest answer is that we need to do both, and that is the work of this chapter.

Start with a simple idea. Profit is a lagging report card. By the time it prints, the story has already happened on the shop floor. A leading indicator is the thing you can watch before the report card arrives, like a farmer checking cloud cover before the harvest tally. For Greaves we picked six such clouds. How many electric scooters did the Ampere plant bill, and what share of new registrations did they win? How much does each scooter still lose? How fast are the medium-sized generator sets selling? How quickly are three-wheeler engines leaving for the assembly lines? How much of every rupee of sales is eaten by metal? And is stock piling up in the warehouse before it turns into cash?

The first pair tells the story of the electric subsidiary. In the September quarter it billed 37,649 scooters, more than double a year earlier, and its share of registrations edged up to 4.8 percent for the half-year. Each scooter lost about 6,300 rupees at the EBITDA level, down from about 20,000 a year ago. EBITDA, in plain words, is operating profit before depreciation and interest. Think of it as the profit a business makes from simply running, before it pays for the machines and the loans. A loss that shrinks by two-thirds while volume doubles is real progress. It is also still a loss, and the plant is working at roughly two-fifths of its capacity.

The second pair belongs to the core. Medium-horsepower generator sets, the 160 to 750 kVA machines that keep hospitals and malls running through a power cut, grew 35 percent in the half-year. Auto engines grew 37 percent in the quarter. Those are strong numbers. Yet the margin that matters fell from 14.8 percent to 11.5 percent. Why? Because aluminium, copper, iron and platinum-group metals all got dearer, and the contracts that let Greaves pass those costs to its customers work with a lag of several months. Management says the full relief arrives in the last quarter of this fiscal year. That is a date, and a date is something we can check.

The sixth cloud is the least glamorous, and often the one that matters most. In the half-year to September, inventories on the balance sheet grew from about 314 crore rupees to about 455 crore. Money owed by customers grew from about 345 crore to about 417 crore. Cash from operations was a negative 212 crore. Part of that is the electric lender, which must put cash out before it earns interest, so you cannot blame all of it on the factories. Still, you and I should notice that a company can grow its sales by a fifth and finish the half-year with less cash than it started with.

There are two smaller dials worth a glance. Excel Controlinkage, the Nagpur maker of cables and gear levers that Greaves bought in stages, shrank 6 percent last year and then grew 14 and 30 percent in the next two quarters, helped by new orders from overseas vehicle, construction-equipment and tractor makers. And the plan to enrol thousands of independent spare-parts retailers has gone quiet. The last firm number was about 350 retailers against a target of 3,000. When a company stops quoting a number it used to be proud of, that silence is a data point too.

Now ask the question every long-term reader should ask: how big can each business get? Here the filings are thinner than we would like. Greaves does not disclose how many engines or generator sets its factories can build, so we cannot compute utilisation for the core. What we do know is that it holds about 4 percent of an industry that makes roughly 1.5 lakh diesel sets a year, led by Mahindra Powerol with about 24 percent. That is a small share in a growing market, which is good news for volume. It is not a moat. The diesel three-wheeler engine, Greaves's best-known product, sits in a market that the rating agency calls continuously shrinking. So the growth has to come from share, from exports and from the parts and service that follow a machine for decades.

The electric plant is the opposite case. It can build 4,80,000 scooters a year and is billing at roughly a third of that pace. Capacity is not the constraint. Dealers, brand and the cost of financing a buyer are. A quick check shows how easily a headline can mislead. Management says utilisation is about 40 percent. But 37,649 scooters over three months is about 12,550 a month, which is about 31 percent of a 40,000-a-month plant. The two figures are probably reconciled by recent months running hotter than the quarter average. Still, it is a reminder to do the small sum yourself.

Which brings us to the heart of the audit: did the people speaking on those calls do what they said? We went through the transcripts from May 2024 to August 2026 and scored every promise whose outcome can be read from a filing. Three were met, five were partly met and two were missed. The missed ones are the telling pair. In May 2024 the finance chief spoke of a standalone return on capital of more than 50 percent; the annual report shows 21 percent. And in early 2025 the board said the electric subsidiary would raise money through a public listing; in July 2026 it dropped the plan and raised 530 crore rupees from its two existing owners instead.

The met promises are just as informative. The company said it would bring the engine business back to a 13 to 15 percent margin, and it has held 13 to 14 percent for three years. It said diesel three-wheelers would hold up better than the electric-switch story implied, and engine revenue has grown more than a third in recent quarters. Do you see the pattern? When the promise is about something the company builds and sells itself, it keeps its word. When the promise depends on a subsidy rule, a commodity price or a capital market, the word is less reliable. That is true of most industrial managements, but it helps to see it in numbers.

Then there is the big number. In early 2025 the board spoke of a vision of 15,000 crore rupees of revenue by 2030, six times the size of the business. The company made 3,437 crore in the year to March 2026. To reach 15,000 crore in four more years it would have to grow about 44.5 percent every year. The stated organic plan is 16 to 20 percent a year. Applied to the core business, that gets you to between 4,825 and 5,526 crore. The rest, between roughly 9,500 and 10,200 crore, must come from the electric subsidiary and from buying other companies. Even if the scooter business grew 40 percent a year, you would still need acquisitions about the size of the whole group today, or some 26 to 28 businesses of the size of Excel Controlinkage.

So what do we make of a management that is candid, mostly accurate about what it controls, silent on dates for what it does not, and attached to a goal the arithmetic does not support? The Russian proverb that Ronald Reagan made famous says trust, but verify. We would trust the 16 to 20 percent core growth ambition, because the first year and a half back it. We would treat the 2030 figure as a flag planted on a distant hill rather than a route. And we would watch three things in the next two quarters: whether the core margin turns up as promised, whether the scooter business posts its first positive EBITDA, and whether cash flow improves without help from suppliers. Those are the places where words become numbers.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Richard Feynman said the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. When a management speaks plainly about its misses, it is tempting to treat the plainness as proof. Candour is a good sign about character. It is not a substitute for a delivered number. The discipline of this chapter is simple: give credit for what has been delivered, write down what is still promised, and check it on the date.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A target that needs 44.5 percent growth every year for four years is not a plan. It is a mood. The useful thing about a mood is that it tells you what the people in the room would like to be true. Read the 15,000 crore vision that way, and read the 16 to 20 percent organic target as the plan.
